title: Sorting by hand
objectives: Implement insertion sort and count its comparisons.
Explain why insertion sort is $O(n^2)$ in the worst case, $O(n)$ on sorted input, and stable.

screens.title: Make room
screens.prose: You hold four cards in order, 2, 5, 7 and 9, and pick up a 6. It sits at the end for now.

state.caption: The first four are in order; 6 is new

screens.question: Tap the cards that must move one place right to make room for the 6.

hints.text: Which of the sorted cards are bigger than 6?
The 6 must end up just right of the last card smaller than it.
7 and 9 are bigger than 6, so both move right. 5 is smaller and stays.

feedback.correct: 7 and 9 move right, and the 6 drops in after the 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move every card bigger than 6, and no others.

byKey.neighbour: You moved only the 9. Then 6 would sit right of 7, out of order.
byKey.all: You moved every card. 2 and 5 are smaller than 6 and can stay.
byKey.c1: You moved the 5. It is smaller than 6, so it stays where it is.
byKey.c0: You moved the 2. It is smaller than 6, so it stays.

explain.text: Walk left from the 6: 9 is bigger, so it shifts; 7 is bigger, so it shifts. 5 is smaller, so we stop and drop the 6 into the gap.

screens.title: One insertion
screens.prose: The first four values are sorted: 2, 4, 5, 6. Take the next value, 1, out of the list. That leaves a gap at index 4. Walk the gap left.
screens.question: Insert 1 into the sorted part, one comparison at a time.

ops.label: Place 1 at index 4
ops.why: You placed 1 right of 6, but 6 is larger. The prefix would no longer be sorted.

ops.label: Place 1 at index 3
ops.why: You placed 1 right of 5, but 5 is larger than 1. Keep shifting.

ops.label: Place 1 at index 2
ops.why: You placed 1 right of 4, but 4 is larger than 1. Keep shifting.

ops.label: Place 1 at index 1
ops.why: You placed 1 right of 2, but 2 is larger than 1. Keep shifting.

ops.label: Compare 1 with index −1
ops.why: There is no index −1. Reaching the left end means 1 is the smallest so far.

w6.tex: 6 > 1\text{, so 1 cannot sit to its right}

w5.tex: 5 > 1\text{, so 1 cannot sit to its right}

w4.tex: 4 > 1\text{, so 1 cannot sit to its right}

w2.tex: 2 > 1\text{, so 1 cannot sit to its right}

hints.text: Compare 1 with the value left of the gap. Is that value bigger?
This is the first value 1 is compared with.
6, 5, 4 and 2 are all bigger than 1, so each shifts right. Then the gap is at index 0: place 1 there.

feedback.correct: Four comparisons, four shifts, and 1 lands at index 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift every bigger value right before placing 1.

byKey.w6: You placed 1 right of 6. 6 is bigger, so it has to shift first.
byKey.w5: You placed 1 right of 5. 5 is bigger than 1, so keep shifting.
byKey.w4: You placed 1 right of 4. 4 is bigger than 1, so keep shifting.
byKey.w2: You placed 1 right of 2. 2 is bigger than 1, so keep shifting.
byKey.wend: You looked for a value left of index 0. There is none, so 1 goes at index 0.

explain.text: Each comparison found a bigger value, so it moved right into the gap. At the left end there was nothing left to compare. The sorted part grew from four values to five.

screens.title: Count the comparisons
screens.prose: This is **insertion sort**: insert each value into the sorted part on its left. Count one comparison each time a value is tested against the key. Reaching the left end is not a comparison.

state.caption: Sort this list from the start

screens.question: Fill in the comparisons for each pass, and the total.

hints.text: For each key, count the values you test before you stop.
Pass 3 inserts 6, and 5 is already smaller.
Key 2: one test, then the left end. Key 4: 5, then 2. Key 6: just 5. Key 1: four tests, then the end. Key 3: 6, 5, 4, then 2 stops it. Total 12.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each test against the key, including the one that stops the walk.

byKey.r1c3: Key 4 is tested against 5 and then against 2. The test that stops the walk counts too.
byKey.r2c3: Key 6 is tested once, against 5, and stops at once.
byKey.r3c3: Key 1 is tested against 6, 5, 4 and 2, then reaches the left end: 4.
byKey.r4c3: Key 3 is tested against 6, 5 and 4, which shift, then against 2, which stops it: 4.

explain.text: A key costs one comparison per value it passes, plus one for the value that stops it. Key 1 passed everything and hit the end, so no stopping test. Here the total is 12.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Return the sorted list and the number of comparisons as a tuple, so the count can be tested. Leave the input list unchanged. Count exactly as before.
screens.question: Write `insertion_sort(xs)`, returning `(sorted_list, comparisons)`.

widget.starter:
def insertion_sort(xs):
    a = list(xs)
    comps = 0
    ...
    return a, comps
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They include the example, an empty list, one value, sorted and reversed lists, duplicates and a nearly sorted list. The last checks that the input is not changed.

hints.text: For each `i` from 1, hold `key = a[i]` and walk `j` left from `i - 1`.
Each test of `a[j] > key` adds 1 to `comps`.
`while j >= 0:` add 1 to `comps`; if `a[j] > key`, set `a[j + 1] = a[j]` and `j -= 1`, else `break`. After the loop, `a[j + 1] = key`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is already sorted and expects 4 comparisons: each new value is compared once with the value before it, then stops.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has duplicates and expects 5. Use `>`, not `>=`: an equal value stops the walk.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 checks the input is unchanged. Sort a copy, `a = list(xs)`.

explain.text: The `break` is what makes the walk stop at the first value not bigger than the key. Without it, every pass would test all the way to the left end.

screens.title: Nearly sorted
screens.prose: A list arrives almost in order: only two neighbouring pairs are swapped.
screens.question: How many comparisons does insertion sort make?

hints.text: Most keys are already bigger than their left neighbour. What does each of those cost?
Key 3 is smaller than 4, so it passes one value before 2 stops it.
Seven keys each cost one stopping test: 7. Keys 3 and 7 each pass one value first: 2 more. Total 9.

feedback.correct: Nine: one per key, plus one per value a key passes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the stopping test for every key, plus the values passed.

byKey.worst: You used the worst case, $8 \times 7 / 2$. The inner loop stops early, so a nearly sorted list is far cheaper.
byKey.nminus1: You counted one test per key. Keys 3 and 7 each pass one value first.
byKey.swaps: You counted only the out-of-order pairs. Every key still needs the test that stops it.

explain.text: Each key costs one stopping test, plus one test per larger value it passes. On a sorted list that is $n - 1$ comparisons, which is $O(n)$. Each swapped pair adds one.

screens.title: The worst case
screens.prose: On a list in reverse order, every key passes every value in the sorted part and reaches the left end. Key $i$ costs $i$ comparisons.
screens.question: How many comparisons does insertion sort make on 1,000 values in reverse order?

hints.text: Add up the cost of each key: $1 + 2 + \dots + 999$.
The upper curve is the reversed list.

feedback.correct: 499,500 comparisons, against 999 on a sorted list.

byKey.square: You used $n^2$. Key $i$ passes only the $i$ values left of it, so the sum is about half of that.
byKey.half: You used $n^2/2$. The exact sum is $n(n - 1)/2$, which is 500 less.
byKey.best: You gave the sorted case. A reversed list makes every key walk to the left end.

explain.text: The worst case is $n(n-1)/2$, which is $O(n^2)$. The best case, a sorted list, is $n - 1$, which is $O(n)$. Doubling the length roughly quadruples the worst case.

screens.title: Always the long way
screens.question: Why does it make 15 comparisons on a list that is already sorted?

options.text: The inner loop never stops early, so every key is tested all the way to the left

options.why: You blamed the pair. `a[j - 1]` and `a[j]` are the right two; the loop just carries on after they are in order.
You blamed the swaps. On a sorted list there are none; the extra cost is comparisons.
The output is sorted. The problem is the time it takes.

hints.text: When `a[j - 1] <= a[j]`, what does the loop do next?
15 is $6 \times 5 / 2$, the reversed-list cost.
With no `break`, the inner loop always runs `i` times. That totals $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$ whatever the input.

feedback.correct: Without a `break`, it is $O(n^2)$ even on sorted input.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what happens once a key is in place.

byKey.neighbour: You blamed the comparison. It is the right pair; the loop simply never stops after it.
byKey.swap: You blamed swapping. A sorted list needs no swaps at all, yet it still makes 15 comparisons.
byKey.order: You doubted the result. It is sorted; it just always does the worst-case work.

explain.text: Once `a[j - 1] <= a[j]`, everything further left is in order too, so the loop should stop. Add `else: break`. Then a sorted list costs 5 comparisons, not 15.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
```python
for i in range(1, len(a)):
    key, j = a[i], i - 1
    while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:
        a[j + 1] = a[j]    # shift right
        j -= 1
    a[j + 1] = key
```

Worst case $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons, $O(n^2)$; sorted input $n - 1$, $O(n)$. It sorts in place. Python's own `sorted` is Timsort: $O(n \log n)$.

state.caption: Two trades at £101: A (index 0) arrived before B (index 2)

screens.question: After insertion sort by price, which £101 trade comes first?

options.why: B stops when it meets A, because `a[j] > key` is False for equal prices. So B never passes A.

options.text: It depends on the other values
options.why: Equal keys never pass each other with `>`, whatever else is in the list.

feedback.correct: Equal values keep their order: insertion sort is **stable**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does `>` let an equal value pass?

explain.text: The shift happens only when `a[j] > key`, so an equal value stops the walk. Equal items keep their arrival order: that is **stability**. With `>=` it would no longer be stable.

screens.title: A day's trades
screens.prose: Trades from a feed arrive almost in time order. Each is `(time, trade_id)`. Sort them by time only, and keep trades with equal times in arrival order.
screens.question: Write `sort_trades(trades)`: a new list sorted by time, stable for equal times.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. They include the feed above, an empty list, one trade, two trades at the same time and a reversed burst. The last checks that the input is not changed.

hints.text: Use insertion sort, but compare only the times, `a[j][0] > key[0]`.
c and e share a time; c arrived first, so c must stay first.
Copy the list. For each key, shift while `a[j][0] > key[0]`, then place the key. Comparing whole tuples would order equal times by id instead.

feedback.correct: Sorted by time, with c before e and b before d.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 has y before x at the same time and expects that order kept. Comparing whole tuples sorted them by id.
byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects c before e. Compare times only, with `>`, so equal times never pass each other.

explain.text: Each late trade walks back only a step or two, so the sort is close to $O(n)$ here. `sorted(trades, key=lambda t: t[0])` gives the same result: Timsort is stable too, and fast on nearly sorted runs.

screens.title: A new price level
screens.prose: A book keeps 1,000 price levels in a list, sorted from low to high. A new level arrives that belongs three places from the end. We insert it by walking left from the end, as insertion sort does.

state.caption: The top six of 1,000 levels (£); the new level is 99.975

screens.question: How many comparisons does the insertion make?

hints.text: Count the values the new level passes, then the one that stops it.
The new level stops at this value, which is smaller.
It passes 100.01, 99.99 and 99.98: three comparisons. Then 99.97 is smaller: one more. Total 4.

feedback.correct: Four comparisons, whatever the size of the book.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the values passed, plus the stopping test.

byKey.shifts: You counted the three values it passes. The test against 99.97, which stops the walk, counts too.
byKey.all: You scanned the whole book. The walk starts at the end and stops after four tests.
byKey.log: You used binary search. That finds the place in 10 looks, but walking from the end is quicker here.

explain.text: Insertion near the end of a sorted list is cheap: 4 comparisons and 3 shifts. When new levels land near the end, as here, insertion into a sorted list fits an order book well.

ideas: Insertion sort grows a sorted part one value at a time, shifting bigger values right to make room.
A key costs one comparison per value it passes, plus one that stops it: $n - 1$ on sorted input, $n(n-1)/2$ reversed.
Shifting only on `>` keeps equal values in arrival order, so insertion sort is stable.

formula.name: Worst-case comparisons
formula.note: $O(n^2)$ in the worst case, $O(n)$ when nearly sorted.

summary.trap: Without a `break` the inner loop always walks to the left end, so even sorted input costs $O(n^2)$.

quiz.prose: Insertion sort runs on `[3, 1, 2]`, counting each test of a value against the key.
quiz.question: How many comparisons does it make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count key 1, then key 2.

explain.text: Key 1 is tested against 3, then reaches the left end: 1. Key 2 is tested against 3, which shifts, then against 1, which stops it: 2. Total 3.

quiz.question: On which input is it fastest?

options.why: You picked the worst case: every key walks to the left end.
On random input each key walks about halfway, which is still $O(n^2)$.

options.text: It takes the same time on every input
options.why: The inner loop stops early, so the time depends on how sorted the input is.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does each key stop at once?

explain.text: On sorted input every key stops at its first test, so 9,999 comparisons. Reverse order costs about 50 million.

options.why: You counted a comparison for the only value. With one value the outer loop never runs.
The value is kept; a list of one is already sorted.
`range(1, 1)` is empty, so nothing is indexed.

feedback.correct: One value, already sorted, no comparisons.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does the outer loop run at all?

explain.text: The outer loop is `range(1, 1)`, which is empty. Nothing is compared and the list comes back as it was.

quiz.prose: You call Python's `sorted` on a million random prices.
quiz.question: How does its time grow with $n$ in the worst case?

options.why: You assumed `sorted` is insertion sort. It is Timsort, which merges runs.
That is the best case, for input already in order or in strictly falling order. On random prices Timsort needs $O(n \log n)$.
Every value must be looked at, so no sort can beat $O(n)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which algorithm does `sorted` use?

explain.text: `sorted` and `list.sort` use Timsort: $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case and stable. It uses insertion sort only on short runs.
